front: Define the **centre of mass** of a system of bodies.
back:
The **centre of mass** is the single point at which the total mass of the system can be taken to act as one.

It is therefore the point through which the whole weight, $W = m g$, of the system acts.

front:
Particles of masses $m_{i}$ lie along the $x$-axis at the points `\left( x_{i}, 0 \right)`. Fill in the blanks to complete the equation for their centre of mass:

`\sum m_{i}x_{i} = \_\_\_\_\_\_ \sum \_\_\_\_\_\_`
back:
The completed equation is:

$\sum m_{i} x_{i} = \overline{x} \sum m_{i}$

The left-hand side adds up each mass multiplied by its position, and the right-hand side is the total mass placed at the centre of mass.

front: Particles lie in a two-dimensional plane rather than along a line. What are the two equivalent ways of finding their centre of mass?
back:
Use **position vectors**: with $r_{i} = x_{i} i + y_{i} j$, solve $\sum m_{i} r_{i} = \overline{r} \sum m_{i}$.

Or treat the two dimensions **separately**, as two straight-line problems, one giving $\overline{x}$ and the other $\overline{y}$.

front: Tins of paint are placed at points along a plank of wood. When can the plank itself be left out of the calculation?
back:
Only when the plank is modelled as **light**, so that it has no mass to contribute.

Any object connecting the particles has its own mass and its own centre of mass, so unless it is light it shifts the answer and must be included.

front: A question gives no axes or origin. What must you do, and what does that mean for your answer?
back:
Create your own axes and origin, and make clear on the diagram where the origin is.

The coordinates of the centre of mass are measured **from that origin**, so a bare pair of numbers means nothing until the origin is stated: the answer is normally given as a distance from a named point.

front: Three lights of masses 5 kg, 7 kg and 8 kg hang from a light rod at 15 cm, 35 cm and 55 cm from one end. How far from that end is their centre of mass?
back:
Multiply each mass by its position, add, and divide by the total mass:

$\frac{5\times15+7\times35+8\times55}{5+7+8} = \frac{760}{20} = 38 \text{cm}$

The rod is light, so it contributes nothing, and 38 cm sits sensibly between the lights and nearer the heavy end.

front: A 2.4 kg particle is at $( - 3 , - 2 )$ and a 7.6 kg particle is at $( p , q )$. Given that the centre of mass is at $( 0 . 04 , 3 . 32 )$, find $p$ and $q$.
back:
Write one equation for each coordinate, using the total mass of 10 kg:

`2.4 \times \left( -3 \right) + 7.6p = 10 \times 0.04`

That gives $7 . 6 p = 7 . 6$, so $p = 1$; the same working vertically gives $7 . 6 q = 38$, so $q = 5$.

front:
**True or False?**

The centre of mass of a system of particles always lies between the outermost particles.
back:
**True.**

The centre of mass is a **weighted average** of the particles' positions, and an average can never fall outside the range of the values it averages.

That makes it a useful check: an answer beyond the outermost particle is certainly wrong.

front: Define a **lamina**.
back:
A **lamina** is a body with one dimension very small compared with the other two, so that the third dimension is negligible.

It is therefore modelled as a flat, two-dimensional plane: a sheet of card, a sheet of metal or a wall.

front: What does it mean for a lamina to be **uniform**?
back:
**Uniform** means the mass per unit area is the same at every point of the lamina.

Its mass is therefore proportional to its area, which is what allows areas to be used in place of masses.

front: A uniform lamina has one or more axes of symmetry. What does that tell you about its centre of mass?
back:
The centre of mass must lie **on** an axis of symmetry.

If the shape has more than one axis of symmetry, the centre of mass is at the **point where they intersect**, which locates it completely with no calculation at all.

front: What is a **median** of a triangle, and where along it is the centre of mass of a uniform triangular lamina?
back:
A **median** joins a vertex to the **midpoint of the opposite side**.

The centre of mass lies $\frac{2}{3}$ of the way along a median, measured **from the vertex**, and equivalently at the point where the three medians meet.

front: The three vertices of a uniform triangular lamina are known. What is the quickest route to its centre of mass, and does it work for other polygons?
back:
Take the **mean of the coordinates of the three vertices**, averaging the $x$ values and the $y$ values separately.

It works only for **triangles**, and is not true for polygons in general.

front: In an isosceles triangular lamina, why do you only need one of the three medians?
back:
Because in an isosceles triangle one of the medians is also an **axis of symmetry**, and the centre of mass has to lie on it.

In an equilateral triangle all three medians are axes of symmetry, so any one of them will do.

An axis of symmetry is perpendicular to the side it bisects, so missing lengths along it can be found by Pythagoras' theorem.

front:
**True or False?**

A semicircle is a sector of a circle.
back:
**True.**

A semicircle is the special case of a sector in which the angle at the centre is $π$ radians.

So any result stated for a sector can be applied to a semicircle, with $π$ as the angle at the centre.

front: Define a **composite lamina**.
back:
A **composite lamina** is a lamina of non-standard shape that can be constructed from two or more **standard** uniform laminas.

An L-shaped shelf made from two rectangles is a typical example.

front: How do you find the centre of mass of a composite lamina made from a single uniform material?
back:
Split it into standard laminas and find the **area** and the **centre of mass** of each one.

Then treat each part as a **particle whose mass is its area**, placed at that part's centre of mass, and use the centre-of-mass equation on those particles.

front: Why may areas be used in place of masses when every part is cut from the same uniform material?
back:
Because the mass of each part is its area multiplied by the mass per unit area, and that constant is the **same for every part**.

It therefore appears in every term on both sides of the equation and **cancels**, leaving only the areas.

front: A circle is cut out of a triangular lamina. How is the removed part handled?
back:
Give it a **negative area**.

It then subtracts in the numerator and in the total, exactly as removing it from the shape subtracts from both the moment and the mass.

front: A triangular lamina of area 28 with centre of mass `\left( \frac{11}{3}, 5 \right)` has a circle of area $π$ and centre $( 3 , 5 )$ removed. Find the centre of mass of what remains.
back:
Both centres lie on $y = 5$, which is an axis of symmetry of the result, so $\overline{y} = 5$ can be written down.

For the other coordinate, take the circle's area as negative:

$\overline{x} = \frac{28\times\frac{11}{3}-3π}{28-π} = 3 . 75$

So the centre of mass is at $( 3 . 75 , 5 )$ to 3 significant figures.

front:
**True or False?**

The material joining the parts of a composite lamina is ignored when finding its centre of mass.
back:
**True.**

Any material used to join the laminas together is modelled as having **negligible** mass, so it contributes nothing.

The composite is also modelled as flat, since its third dimension is small compared with the other two.

front: Which four standard uniform laminas is a composite lamina built from?
back:
**Rectangles** (including squares), **triangles**, **circles** and **sectors** (including semicircles).

Each of these has a centre of mass that can be written down or looked up, which is exactly why the shape is split into them.

front: Define a **framework**.
back:
A **framework** is a flat shape created by joining thin, linear bodies together.

Those bodies are modelled as **rods** or **wires**: the supporting structure of a roof, or four rope lights joined into a rectangle.

front: How does finding the centre of mass of a framework differ from doing it for a composite lamina?
back:
A framework has no area to divide up, so you work with its **perimeter** instead.

Identify the individual rods, and treat each one as a particle whose mass is its **length**, rather than splitting a region into standard shapes with areas.

front: A framework includes a curved rod. What shape will it be, and what is its length?
back:
At this level a curved rod is always a **circular arc**.

Its length is $l = r θ$, where $r$ is the radius and $θ$ is the angle at the centre, measured in **radians**.

front: The formula booklet gives one centre-of-mass result for a circular **arc** and another for a **sector**. Which object does each describe?
back:
The **arc** result, $\frac{r\mathrm{sin}α}{α}$ from the centre, is for a wire bent into an arc, so it belongs to a **framework**.

The **sector** result, $\frac{2r\mathrm{sin}α}{3α}$ from the centre, is for the solid **lamina**, the arc together with the two radii and the region between them.

The booklet lists the lamina and framework results together, so the two lines are easy to confuse.

front:
The formula booklet gives the centre of mass of a circular arc of radius $r$ as $\frac{r\mathrm{sin}α}{α}$ from the centre. Fill in the blanks:

the angle at the centre of the arc is `\_\_\_\_\_\_`, and $α$ is measured in `\_\_\_\_\_\_`.
back:
The completed statement is:

the angle at the centre of the arc is $2 α$, and $α$ is measured in **radians**.

So $α$ is **half** the angle at the centre, not the whole of it: a semicircular wire has $2 α = π$ and therefore $α = \frac{π}{2}$.

front: A sector-shaped wire sign has two straight wires of length 60 cm and an arc, with an angle of $\frac{π}{3}$ at the centre. What three lengths go into the calculation?
back:
The two straight wires, 60 cm each, and the arc.

The arc's length is $l = r θ = 60 \times \frac{π}{3} = 20 π \approx 62 . 8 \text{cm}$, using the full angle at the centre.

front: Where is a straight rod's own centre of mass taken to be, and how do you find the length of a sloping one?
back:
At the **midpoint** of the rod, so its coordinates are the mean of the coordinates of the rod's two ends.

A sloping rod's length comes from **Pythagoras' theorem** on its horizontal and vertical extents, for example $\sqrt{8^{2}+6^{2}} = 10$.

front: A lamina hangs freely in equilibrium from a fixed point. Which two forces act on it, and where does each one act?
back:
The **tension** in the string, acting at the fixed point of suspension.

The **weight**, acting at the lamina's **centre of mass**.

front: What is the key geometric fact about a freely suspended object at rest?
back:
The **point of suspension** and the **centre of mass** lie on the same **vertical** line.

The only two forces acting are the tension and the weight, and two forces can balance only if they act along one line, so that line must be the vertical through both points.

front: How do you find the angle between the string and a named edge of a suspended lamina?
back:
Mark the centre of mass and draw the vertical line joining it to the point of suspension, then identify the angle the question asks for.

It comes out of **trigonometry** on the right-angled triangle whose two shorter sides are the horizontal and vertical distances between those two points.

front: A lamina is free to rotate about a pivot on its surface instead of hanging from a string. What changes, and what does not?
back:
The tension is replaced by a **reaction force** acting at the pivot.

The geometry is unchanged: the pivot and the centre of mass still end up on the same vertical line, and the trigonometry that follows is identical.

Only the wording of the question really differs.

front:
Fill in the blanks to complete what equilibrium means for a suspended object:

there is zero resultant `\_\_\_\_\_\_` acting on it, and zero resultant `\_\_\_\_\_\_` about the point of suspension.
back:
The completed statement is:

there is zero resultant **force** acting on it, and zero resultant **moment** about the point of suspension.

It is the second condition that fixes the object's orientation, rather than merely holding it up.

front: Before finding the angle, what must you already have, and why must you settle whether the object is a lamina or a framework?
back:
You must already have the position of the **centre of mass**, since the whole construction hangs off it.

The method for finding it is not the same for the two kinds of object, so getting the type wrong gives the wrong centre of mass and therefore the wrong angle.

front: Where does the vertical line through the centre of mass fall when a lamina on a slope is stable, on the point of tipping, or toppling?
back:
**Stable:** the line passes through the edge that is **in contact** with the plane, and the lamina rests in equilibrium.

**On the point of tipping:** it passes exactly through the **vertex** of that edge closest to where the plane meets the horizontal.

**Toppling:** it falls **outside** that edge, passing through an edge not in contact with the plane.

front: What axes suit a tipping problem, and where does the origin go?
back:
The $x$-axis runs **parallel** to the inclined plane and the $y$-axis **perpendicular** to it.

The origin goes at the vertex of the lamina that is in contact with the plane and closest to where the plane meets the horizontal, the "bottom left" corner.

front: A lamina rests on a rough inclined plane. What is the main modelling assumption in a tipping problem?
back:
That the **friction** between the lamina and the plane is great enough to stop it **sliding**, however steep the plane is made.

Toppling is then the only thing that can happen, so the question becomes purely one about where the centre of mass sits.

front:
A lamina on a slope has its centre of mass at `\left( \overline{x}, \overline{y} \right)`, measured parallel and perpendicular to the plane from the lower vertex. Fill in the blanks to complete the tipping condition:

`\tan\theta = \frac{\_\_\_\_\_\_}{\_\_\_\_\_\_}`
back:
The completed condition is:

$\mathrm{tan} θ = \frac{\overline{x}}{\overline{y}}$

The two coordinates are the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse joins the lower vertex to the centre of mass, and at the moment of tipping that hypotenuse is vertical.

front: A symmetrical T-shaped lamina has its centre of mass at $( 6 , 6 )$, measured from the lower vertex. At what angle of slope does it topple?
back:
Substitute into the tipping condition:

$\mathrm{tan} θ = \frac{6}{6} = 1$

So $θ = 45 ^{\circ}$, and the plane can be raised to $45 ^{\circ}$ before the lamina topples.

front:
**True or False?**

A carefully drawn diagram will tell you whether a lamina on a slope topples.
back:
**False.**

A diagram cannot be relied on to show whether the vertical through the centre of mass falls inside or outside the edge in contact with the plane, because the two cases can look almost identical.

The diagram is there to set the problem up; the verdict has to come from trigonometry.

front: Define **non-uniform**, as the term is used for laminas and frameworks here.
back:
It means that the separate parts may have **different densities** from one another, while **each individual part is still uniform** in itself.

It does not mean that the density varies from point to point within a single lamina or a single rod.

front: Part of a uniform lamina is folded back on itself. Why does that make it non-uniform, and how is the folded part handled?
back:
The folded region is now **two layers thick**, so it has twice the density of the rest and the lamina is no longer uniform.

Use **double the area** for that region, and treat the result as an ordinary composite lamina.

front: A framework is made from rods of different thicknesses. How is that given to you, and what do you do with it?
back:
The question states the **relationship** between them, for instance that one cable is twice as thick as the others.

Scale the **lengths** in the same ratio, so a rod of double thickness counts as double its length.

front: Spotlights are attached to a framework of metal rods. How do they enter the calculation?
back:
Each one enters as an extra **particle**, placed at its point of attachment and carrying its own mass.

It is added alongside the rods in the centre-of-mass equation, and it moves the centre of mass towards itself.

front: A sign hangs horizontally in equilibrium from two strings. What decides the tensions in them?
back:
The **position of the centre of mass**, since that is where the whole weight acts.

Taking moments about one attachment point gives the tension at the other, and resolving vertically then gives the first.

The string nearer the centre of mass carries the greater tension.

front:
**True or False?**

To handle a non-uniform object you need the actual density of each part.
back:
**False.**

Only the **ratio** between the densities is needed, which is why a question gives you a relationship such as "twice as thick" rather than any numbers.

The constant of proportionality appears in every term on both sides of the centre-of-mass equation and cancels, so the answer depends on the relative weighting alone.

front: How is impulse written for a constant force in two dimensions?
back:
In exactly the same way, with the force and the impulse as **vectors**: $I = F t$, so a force `\left( F_{x}\mathbf{i} + F_{y}\mathbf{j} \right)` N acting for $t$ seconds gives `\mathbf{I} = \left( F_{x}\mathbf{i} + F_{y}\mathbf{j} \right)t`.

The units are unchanged: newton seconds, N s.

front:
A particle of mass $m$ kg has velocity $u$ before an impulse and $v$ after it. Fill in the blank to complete the impulse-momentum principle in vector form:

`\mathbf{I} = \_\_\_\_\_\_`
back:
The completed principle is:

`\mathbf{I} = m\left( \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u} \right)`

Subtract the velocity **vectors** first, component by component, and only then multiply by the mass.

front: A 0.8 kg ball's velocity changes from `\left( 2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} \right)` to `\left( 5\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} \right)\text{ m s}^{-1}`. Find the magnitude of the impulse it received.
back:
Take the change in velocity and multiply by the mass:

`\mathbf{I} = 0.8\left( 3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} \right) = \left( 2.4\mathbf{i} - 3.2\mathbf{j} \right)\text{ N s}`

Its magnitude is $\sqrt{2.4^{2}+3.2^{2}} = 4 \text{N s}$.

front: How do you find the direction of an impulse vector, and what must you check in the question first?
back:
Find its two components, sketch them as the sides of a right-angled triangle, and use trigonometry on that triangle.

Check **where the angle is measured from**, since a question may ask for the angle with $i$, with $j$, or as a bearing, and the three answers differ.

front: An impulse is `\left( 2.4\mathbf{i} - 3.2\mathbf{j} \right)` N s. Find the angle between it and the vector $j$.
back:
Sketching it shows the impulse pointing right and **downwards**, so the angle from $j$ must be more than $90 ^{\circ}$.

The angle below the horizontal is `\tan^{-1}\left( \frac{3.2}{2.4} \right) = 53.1^{\circ}`, so the angle from $j$ is $90 ^{\circ} + 53 . 1 ^{\circ} = 143 ^{\circ}$ to 3 significant figures.

front:
**True or False?**

If two particles collide directly in two dimensions, their velocity vectors are scalar multiples of one another.
back:
**True.**

A **direct** collision means both particles travel along the same straight line, so every velocity vector points along that one line and can differ only by a scalar factor.

The problem then reduces to conservation of momentum worked exactly as it would be in one dimension.

front: You are given an impulse by its magnitude and direction rather than by its components. What must you do before using it?
back:
**Resolve** it into horizontal and vertical components.

The vector arithmetic, adding and subtracting and applying the impulse-momentum principle, all works component by component, so the magnitude and direction have to be converted first.

front: After two objects collide, what else might one of them hit, and how do you handle it?
back:
It may go on to hit a **third object**, or a **wall** perpendicular to its motion.

Deal with **each collision separately**, applying the usual before-and-after method to one collision at a time and carrying its results forward into the next.

front: Balls A, B and C lie on one line, A hits B, and then B hits C. What are the three ways A and B can collide a second time?
back:
One of them is **stationary** and the other is travelling towards it.

Both are travelling in **opposite directions**, towards each other.

Both are travelling in the **same direction**, and the one in front is the slower of the two.

front: After bouncing off a wall, when does a ball catch the one ahead of it?
back:
When its velocity in that direction is **greater** than the other ball's velocity in the same direction.

The wall reverses the ball's direction, so it is now travelling back towards the other one, but it only reaches it if it is also gaining on it.

front: To find a ball's speed after it hits a wall, what extra information will the question give you?
back:
Either the **impulse** the wall exerted on the ball, or the **coefficient of restitution** between the ball and the wall.

One or the other is needed because the wall does not move, so there is no second velocity to put into a conservation of momentum equation.

front: After a chain of collisions, A moves forwards at $1 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and B, which is ahead of it, moves forwards at $0 . 25 \text{m s}^{-1}$. Will they collide again?
back:
**Yes.**

Both are travelling in the same direction and the one in front, B, is the slower, so the gap between them is closing at $0 . 75 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and A must catch it.

front:
**True or False?**

A chain of collisions needs one equation for each collision, rather than a single equation for the whole chain.
back:
**True.**

Each collision introduces new unknown velocities, so it has to be solved on its own with a before-and-after diagram before you move on to the next one.

Working the collisions in order is also what tells you which objects are where, and so which of them can meet again.

front: Define the **coefficient of restitution**.
back:
The **coefficient of restitution**, written $e$, measures how bouncy a collision between two particular objects is, and is also known as **Newton's law of restitution**.

It is a ratio, so it is **dimensionless**, and its value depends on the materials the two objects are made from.

front: What range of values can $e$ take, and what happens at each end of it?
back:
$0 \leq e \leq 1$.

At $e = 1$ the collision is **perfectly elastic** and no kinetic energy is lost.

At $e = 0$ it is **perfectly inelastic**, and the two objects coalesce and move off together.

front:
**True or False?**

Two objects moving the same way at $5$ and $2 \text{m s}^{-1}$ have a speed of approach of $7 \text{m s}^{-1}$.
back:
**False.**

Moving in the same direction they close on each other by $5 - 2 = 3$ metres every second, so the speed of approach is $3 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

It would be $5 + 2 = 7 \text{m s}^{-1}$ only if they were travelling in **opposite** directions.

front:
Two objects have velocities $u_{1}$ and $u_{2}$ before a collision and $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ after it. Fill in the blanks to complete the coefficient of restitution:

`e = \frac{\_\_\_\_\_\_}{\_\_\_\_\_\_}`
back:
The completed formula is:

$e = \frac{v_{2}-v_{1}}{u_{1}-u_{2}}$

In words, that is the **speed of separation** divided by the **speed of approach**; the velocities may be negative, so watch the signs rather than trusting the order of the letters.

front: How does the formula simplify when an object bounces off a wall?
back:
The wall has no velocity of its own, so the ratio becomes the **speed of rebound** divided by the **speed of approach**.

For an object arriving at $u$ and leaving at $v$ that is simply $e = \frac{v}{u}$.

front: A (2 kg) at $9 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and B (5 kg) at $1 \text{m s}^{-1}$ move the same way and collide, with $e = \frac{3}{4}$. Find their speeds afterwards.
back:
Restitution gives the speed of separation as `\frac{3}{4} \times \left( 9 - 1 \right) = 6`, so $v_{2} - v_{1} = 6$, and momentum gives $2 \times 9 + 5 \times 1 = 2 v_{1} + 5 v_{2}$.

Solving the pair gives $v_{1} = - 1$ and $v_{2} = 5$.

So A has reversed and moves back at $1 \text{m s}^{-1}$, while B goes on at $5 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

front: A question leaves a velocity in terms of $e$, such as $v = 5 e - 1$. How does that give you a range of possible values of $e$?
back:
Use what the question tells you about the **direction** of travel: if that object must be moving forwards its velocity is positive, so $5 e - 1 > 0$ and therefore $e > \frac{1}{5}$.

Combine that with $0 \leq e \leq 1$, which always holds, to get the full range: $\frac{1}{5} < e \leq 1$.

front:
A particle's acceleration varies with time, so the suvat formulae cannot be used. Fill in the blanks to complete the calculus links:

Differentiate `\_\_\_\_\_\_` to get velocity, and differentiate velocity to get `\_\_\_\_\_\_`
back:
The completed link is:

Differentiate **displacement** to get velocity, and differentiate velocity to get **acceleration**.

Integrating runs the same chain backwards: integrate acceleration to get velocity, and integrate velocity to get displacement.

Each of the three is a function of time, and differentiating measures a **rate of change** with respect to time.

front: On a velocity-time graph that is a **curve**, how do you find the acceleration at a particular moment, and the displacement over an interval?
back:
**Differentiate** to find the acceleration at a moment, and **integrate** to find the displacement over an interval.

Because the graph curves, the gradient differs at every point and the region under it is not made of triangles and rectangles whose areas can simply be added.

Calculus does both jobs: the derivative gives the gradient at a point, and the definite integral gives the area under the curve.

front: A kinematics question says a particle **starts from rest**. What does that tell you, and what do you use it for?
back:
Starting from rest means the velocity is zero at the start, so $v = 0$ when $t = 0$.

That is a pair of matching values, exactly what is needed to find the **constant of integration**: substitute both into the expression after integrating and solve for the constant.

The word **initially** does the same job on its own: it means $t = 0$.

front: A particle's velocity changes sign between $t = 0$ and $t = 3$. Why does `\int_{0}^{3} v \text{ d}t` not give the distance it has travelled?
back:
That integral gives the **displacement**, not the distance.

While the velocity is negative the particle is moving backwards, and the integral counts that motion as negative, so it subtracts from the total instead of adding to it.

To find the distance, first find the times when $v = 0$, the moments the particle turns round, then integrate between each consecutive pair and add the **sizes** of the results, ignoring their signs.

front:
**True or False?**

You can assume that integrating a particle's acceleration between two times gives its velocity at the later time.
back:
**False.**

Integrating acceleration between two times gives the **change** in velocity over that interval, not the velocity itself.

To get the velocity at the later time, add that change to the velocity at the earlier time.

The two only happen to agree when the particle was at rest at the earlier time, since then the change and the final velocity are the same number.

front: A particle's velocity is given as $v = 3 \text{e}^{0.5t}$ rather than as a polynomial. What changes about the way you find its displacement?
back:
Nothing about the method changes: the displacement is still found by integrating the velocity, and the constant of integration is still found by substituting a known pair of values.

Only the **integration itself** is different, because a different technique is needed for an exponential than for a polynomial.

The links between displacement, velocity and acceleration do not depend on what kind of function of $t$ you have been given.

front: How do you differentiate or integrate a vector in kinematics?
back:
Work on **each component separately**.

To differentiate, differentiate the $i$ component and the $j$ component; to integrate, integrate each of them.

The links between displacement, velocity and acceleration are the same as in one dimension, and only the displacement changes name: in two dimensions it is usually written $r$ rather than $s$.

front:
**True or False?**

You can assume that the constant of integration in a two-dimensional kinematics problem is a single number.
back:
**False.**

Integrating a vector gives a **vector** constant of integration, with an $i$ component and a $j$ component.

Find it by substituting a known vector and then equating the $i$ components and the $j$ components separately, which gives one equation for each part of the constant.

So, for example, integrating a velocity might give $r = t^{2} i + 2 \text{e}^{0.5t} j + c$, and a starting position of `\left(3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}\right)\text{ m}` then gives `\mathbf{c} = \left(3\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}\right)\text{ m}`.

front: A particle's position vector is $r$ and its displacement from where it started is $s$. How are the two related, and why are they not the same thing?
back:
They are related by $r = r_{0} + s$, where $r_{0}$ is the particle's **initial position** vector.

They differ because $s$ is measured from **wherever the particle started**, while $r$ is measured from the **origin**, and a particle need not start at the origin.

When you integrate a velocity to find the position, $r_{0}$ is exactly what the constant of integration turns out to be.

front: A particle's velocity is `\left(3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}\right)\text{ m s}^{-1}`. What is its speed?
back:
Its speed is $5  \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Speed is the **magnitude** of the velocity, so it comes from Pythagoras' theorem on the two components:

`\left|\mathbf{v}\right| = \sqrt{3^{2} + \left(- 4\right)^{2}} = 5 \textrm{ }\text{m s}^{- 1}`

The same move applied to a displacement gives the **distance** from the starting point; both are single numbers and neither can be negative.

front: A question asks which direction a particle is moving in. Which vector do you use, and why not the position vector?
back:
Use the **velocity**: the position vector says where the particle **is**, measured from the origin.

The velocity says where it is **heading**, and the two need not point the same way: a particle can be north-east of the origin while travelling due south.

The direction of the velocity may then be wanted as an angle, as a bearing, or as a vector that the velocity is parallel to.

front: Define a **projectile**.
back:
A **projectile** is a particle moving freely under gravity in a two-dimensional plane.

A thrown ball, a javelin and an arrow are all modelled this way.

front:
A projectile is launched with initial speed $U$ at an angle $θ$ to the horizontal. Fill in the blanks to complete the components of its initial velocity:

horizontal: `u_{x} = U \_\_\_\_\_\_`

vertical: `u_{y} = U \_\_\_\_\_\_`
back:
The completed components are:

horizontal: $u_{x} = U \mathrm{cos} θ$

vertical: $u_{y} = U \mathrm{sin} θ$

The **cosine** goes with the horizontal component because that component is the side **adjacent** to the angle in the right-angled triangle, with $U$ as the hypotenuse.

front: How is the acceleration of a projectile written as a single two-dimensional vector?
back:
Taking upwards as positive, it is `\left( 0\mathbf{i} - g\mathbf{j} \right)\text{ m s}^{-2}`.

Writing it this way makes the point of the whole topic explicit: only one of the two components is non-zero, so only the vertical motion is ever accelerated.

front: A question gives a projectile's initial velocity as a vector rather than as a speed and an angle. How do you recover the speed and the angle of projection?
back:
The initial **speed** is the **magnitude** of that vector, found from Pythagoras' theorem on its two components.

The **angle of projection** comes from a sketch and trigonometry, using the same two components as the sides of a right-angled triangle.

front:
**True or False?**

A projectile launched below the horizontal has a negative angle of projection.
back:
**True.**

The angle is measured from the horizontal, so projecting downwards rather than upwards makes $θ$ negative.

That is exactly what is wanted, because it makes the vertical component of the initial velocity negative, and the projectile does start out moving downwards.

front: A projectile is launched at $25 ^{\circ}$ to the horizontal with speed $5 \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find its initial velocity as a vector.
back:
Resolve the speed into its two components:

`\mathbf{u} = \left( 5\cos 25^{\circ}\mathbf{i} + 5\sin 25^{\circ}\mathbf{j} \right) = \left( 4.53\mathbf{i} + 2.11\mathbf{j} \right)\text{ m s}^{-1}`

Both components are positive, which says the projectile sets off upwards and to the right.

front: Which modelling assumptions about a projectile make its horizontal acceleration zero?
back:
That there is **no air resistance** and no other horizontal force acting on it, and that its **spin and rotation** are ignored.

With nothing acting horizontally there is nothing to change the horizontal velocity, so it stays constant for the whole flight.

front: How are the constant-acceleration formulae applied to a projectile?
back:
Apply them to the **horizontal and vertical directions separately**, as two one-dimensional problems.

The acceleration is different in each: it is **zero** horizontally, which reduces the horizontal formula to $s = u t$, and it is $- g$ vertically, taking upwards as positive.

Because each direction is treated on its own, $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ can be used here, even though it has no vector form.

front: What single quantity links the horizontal and vertical parts of a projectile problem?
back:
The **time**, $t$.

The two directions are otherwise independent, but the projectile is in flight for one interval of time, so the same $t$ appears in both sets of equations.

That is what makes the problems solvable: a time found from the vertical motion can be substituted into the horizontal motion, and the other way round.

front:
**True or False?**

You can assume that a projectile is momentarily at rest at its highest point.
back:
**False.**

Only the **vertical** component of the velocity is zero there; the **horizontal** component is unchanged, because there is no horizontal acceleration.

So at the highest point the projectile is still moving horizontally, with speed $U \mathrm{cos} θ$, which is the **smallest** speed it has at any point in its flight and is never zero.

An object thrown straight up is the special case that does come to rest, because it has no horizontal component to begin with.

front: How do you find the greatest height a projectile reaches?
back:
Use the fact that the **vertical** component of the velocity is **zero** at that point, and apply a vertical constant-acceleration formula.

With $v = 0$, $u = U \mathrm{sin} θ$ and $a = - g$, the formula $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ gives the vertical displacement directly, without needing the time.

If the projectile was launched from above ground level, that displacement is measured **from the launch point**, so the launch height has to be added to get the height above the ground.

front: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff rather than from ground level. Which of the two directions does the cliff height affect, and which does it not?
back:
It affects the **vertical** direction only.

The horizontal motion is unchanged, because the horizontal acceleration is zero wherever the stone started from, so the horizontal equation is the same as it would be on level ground.

The cliff enters the problem only through the **vertical displacement** at the moment of landing, which is measured from the point of projection rather than from the ground.

front: A projectile is launched and lands at the **same height**. What does the symmetry of its path let you say about the highest point?
back:
The path is symmetrical about the highest point, so the projectile reaches it exactly **halfway** through the motion.

The time to the highest point is therefore **half** the total time of flight, and the horizontal distance to it is **half** the range.

Both of these depend on the launch and landing heights being equal: thrown from a cliff, the path is no longer symmetrical and neither shortcut holds.

front: The constant-acceleration formulae give the horizontal and vertical displacements of a projectile separately. How is the **equation of its trajectory** different?
back:
The two suvat results are **parametric** equations: they give $x$ and $y$ each in terms of the **time**, which acts as the parameter.

The equation of the trajectory is a **Cartesian** equation, linking $x$ and $y$ to each other directly, in the form `y = \text{f} \left(x\right)`, with no time in it at all.

It is obtained by **eliminating the parameter** between the two, exactly as for any pair of parametric equations.

front: When deriving the equation of a trajectory, which of the two displacement equations do you rearrange, and why that one?
back:
Rearrange the **horizontal** equation.

Because there is no horizontal acceleration it is simply `x = \left(U \cos \theta\right) t`, which rearranges to $t = \frac{x}{U\mathrm{cos}θ}$ in one step.

The vertical equation contains $t^{2}$ as well as $t$, so making $t$ its subject would mean solving a quadratic; substituting the horizontal result into the vertical one avoids that entirely.

front: How does the equation of a trajectory show that the path of a projectile is a **parabola**?
back:
The equation is $y = x \mathrm{tan} θ - \frac{gx^{2}}{2U^{2}\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ}$.

For a fixed launch speed and angle, everything except $x$ and $y$ is constant, so this is a quadratic in $x$, and the graph of a quadratic is a parabola.

The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is **negative**, since $g$, $U^{2}$ and $\mathrm{cos}^{2} θ$ are all positive, so the parabola opens **downwards**, which is why the path has a greatest height rather than a least one.

front:
A projectile is launched with speed $U$ at an angle $θ$. Fill in the blanks in the equation of its trajectory:

`y = x \_\_\_\_\_\_ - \frac{g x^{2}}{2 U^{2} \_\_\_\_\_\_}`
back:
The completed equation is:

$y = x \mathrm{tan} θ - \frac{gx^{2}}{2U^{2}\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ}$

The tangent comes from $\frac{U\mathrm{sin}θ}{U\mathrm{cos}θ}$ in the first term, and the $\mathrm{cos}^{2} θ$ from squaring the $U \mathrm{cos} θ$ in the denominator of the substituted time.

front: What can you do with the equation of a trajectory that you cannot do as directly with the two separate displacement equations?
back:
Get straight from a horizontal distance to a height, or from a height to a horizontal distance, **without finding the time first**.

With the parametric pair you would have to find $t$ from one equation and substitute it into the other every time; the trajectory equation has already done that once and for all.

That is what makes it the natural tool for questions asking whether a projectile clears a wall or passes over a given point.

front: What three assumptions do all the standard projectile formulae depend on?
back:
They assume that the **launch and landing points are at the same vertical level**, that the projectile travels **over horizontal ground**, and that **no force acts on it except gravity**.

The first is the one that is most often broken by a question. Anything launched from a cliff, a building or a window lands lower than it started, and the formulae no longer apply.

front: How is the **time of flight** of a projectile derived, and why does the working produce two answers?
back:
Set the vertical displacement to **zero**, since the projectile returns to the level it started from, and use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ vertically:

`0 = \left(U \sin \theta\right) t - \frac{1}{2} g t^{2}`

Factorising gives `0 = t \left(U \sin \theta - \frac{1}{2} g t\right)`, so either $t = 0$ or $t = \frac{2U\mathrm{sin}θ}{g}$.

Two answers appear because the vertical displacement is zero at **two** moments, at the start and at landing; the $t = 0$ root is the launch itself and is rejected.

front: At the maximum height the vertical component of velocity is zero. Which vertical formula gives the **time** to that point, and which gives the **height** itself?
back:
For the **time**, use $v = u + a t$: with $v = 0$, $0 = U \mathrm{sin} θ - g t$, giving $t = \frac{U\mathrm{sin}θ}{g}$.

For the **height**, use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$: with $v = 0$, $0 = U^{2} \mathrm{sin}^{2} θ - 2 g y$, giving $y = \frac{U^{2}\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ}{2g}$.

Choosing between them is the usual suvat choice: the first formula contains $t$ and not $s$, the second contains $s$ and not $t$.

front:
For a projectile launched with speed $U$ at an angle $θ$ over horizontal ground, fill in the blanks:

time of flight `= \frac{2 U \_\_\_\_\_\_}{g}`

range `= \frac{U^{2} \_\_\_\_\_\_}{g}`
back:
The completed formulae are:

time of flight $= \frac{2U\mathrm{sin}θ}{g}$

range $= \frac{U^{2}\mathrm{sin}2θ}{g}$

Note the difference: the time of flight has $\mathrm{sin} θ$, the range has $\mathrm{sin} 2 θ$. The doubled angle appears only in the range, and only because of the identity used at the last step of its derivation.

front: How is the **range** of a projectile derived, and where does the $\mathrm{sin} 2 θ$ come from?
back:
The range is the horizontal distance covered in the whole time of flight, and horizontally there is no acceleration, so $s = u t$ applies:

`x = \left(U \cos \theta\right) \left(\frac{2 U \sin \theta}{g}\right) = \frac{2 U^{2} \sin \theta \cos \theta}{g}`

The double angle identity $2 \mathrm{sin} θ \mathrm{cos} θ = \mathrm{sin} 2 θ$ then turns that into $\frac{U^{2}\mathrm{sin}2θ}{g}$.

So the $\mathrm{sin} 2 θ$ is not a mechanics result at all: it is a trigonometric identity tidying up the answer at the very end.

front:
**True or False?**

You can assume the range formula gives the horizontal distance travelled by a projectile launched from the top of a cliff.
back:
**False.**

Every one of the standard projectile formulae is derived on the assumption that the launch and landing points are at the **same level**, and a cliff breaks that.

A projectile launched from a cliff is in the air for longer than the formula allows for, so it travels further horizontally than the formula predicts.

For a launch and landing at different heights, go back to the constant-acceleration formulae applied to each direction separately.

front: A uniform ladder rests against a rough vertical wall with its foot on rough horizontal ground. Which forces act on the ladder at its two points of contact, and in which directions?
back:
At the **foot** there is a normal reaction from the ground acting **vertically upwards**, and a frictional force acting **horizontally towards the wall**.

At the **top** there is a normal reaction from the wall acting **horizontally**, away from the wall, and a frictional force acting **vertically upwards**.

In each case the friction acts in the direction that opposes the way the ladder would slip.

front: A ladder leans on a peg instead of against a vertical wall. How does the reaction force on it differ?
back:
Against a **vertical wall** the normal reaction is **horizontal**, because a normal reaction acts perpendicular to the surface producing it and that surface is the wall.

On a **peg** the normal reaction acts **perpendicular to the ladder**, because there it is the ladder that is the surface in contact.

front:
**True or False?**

For a ladder resting against a rough wall with its foot on rough ground, you can assume the coefficient of friction is the same at both contacts.
back:
**False.**

The two contacts are between different pairs of surfaces, so their coefficients of friction can be **different**, and a question will give both values if both are needed.

Taking them to be equal is an assumption that has not been made for you.

front:
A ladder is inclined at an angle $θ$ to the horizontal. A force acts at a point a distance $d$ along the ladder from its foot. Fill in the blanks:

If the force is **vertical**, its perpendicular distance from the foot is `\_\_\_\_\_\_`.

If the force is **horizontal**, its perpendicular distance from the foot is `\_\_\_\_\_\_`.
back:
The completed distances for a ladder inclined at $θ$ to the horizontal are:

If the force is **vertical**, its perpendicular distance from the foot is $d \mathrm{cos} θ$.

If the force is **horizontal**, its perpendicular distance from the foot is $d \mathrm{sin} θ$.

The perpendicular distance for a vertical force is measured horizontally, which is why it uses the cosine, and for a horizontal force it is measured vertically, which is why it uses the sine.

front: A rod is freely hinged to a wall at one end. What does that tell you about how the rod can move, and about the force acting on it there?
back:
The hinged end is **fixed** in position, but the rod is **free to rotate** about it.

The wall exerts a single **resultant force** on the rod at the hinge, and that force acts at an **angle** rather than perpendicular to the wall, because it has to prevent the end moving in any direction.

front: For a rod that is freely hinged at one end, why is the hinge usually the best point to take moments about?
back:
Because the force from the hinge acts **through** the hinge, so its moment about that point is zero and it disappears from the equation.

That matters more here than it does elsewhere, because the hinge force is unknown in **both** magnitude and direction, so avoiding it removes two unknowns at once.

front: You have found the horizontal and vertical components of the force exerted by a hinge on a rod. How do you give the magnitude and the direction of that force?
back:
The magnitude of the hinge force is found using Pythagoras:

`|R| = \sqrt{R_{H}^{2} + R_{V}^{2}}`

The direction is found using right-angled trigonometry:

`\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{R_{V}}{R_{H}}\right)`

where $α$ is the angle the force makes above the horizontal.

front: A rod is held horizontally at a wall. What is the difference between the forces acting on it if it is hinged to the wall and if it is simply in contact with the wall?
back:
If it is **hinged**, the wall exerts one **resultant force** at an angle, and that is what stops the rod rotating about the hinge.

If it is **simply in contact**, the wall exerts a **normal reaction** perpendicular to the wall together with a **frictional force** acting up the wall, and that is what stops the rod sliding down.

Resolving the hinge's resultant force into horizontal and vertical components makes the two situations mathematically the same.

front: In mechanics, define the **work done** by a force.
back:
**Work is done** by a force when that force causes the object to move: both a force and movement are needed.

A force that merely holds an object stationary does no work at all, however large it is.

front:
A force of magnitude $F$ N acts at an angle $θ$ to the direction of motion while the object moves a distance $d$ m. Fill in the blank to complete the work done:

`W = Fd\_\_\_\_\_\_`
back:
The completed formula is:

$W = F d \mathrm{cos} θ$

Only the **component of the force in the direction of motion** counts, and that component is $F \mathrm{cos} θ$.

front: An object is pushed up an inclined plane. Which of the forces acting on it does no work, and why?
back:
The **normal reaction**.

Work counts only the component of a force **in the direction of motion**, and the normal reaction acts perpendicular to the plane, so it has no component along the slope at all.

front:
**True or False?**

1 joule is the work done by a force of 1 newton moving an object 1 metre.
back:
**True**, provided the metre is measured **along the line of action** of the force.

That is also why work can be measured in **newton metres**, and why $1 \text{J} = 1 \text{N m}$.

Larger amounts are given in kilojoules, with $1 \text{kJ} = 1000 \text{J}$.

front: A box is dragged along a rough floor at **constant speed**. What does the constant speed tell you, and how much work is done against friction?
back:
Constant speed means zero acceleration, so the forces along the direction of motion **balance**: the forward component of the pull equals the frictional force.

The work done against friction is then that frictional force multiplied by the distance moved.

front: A child pulls a box 5 m along a rough floor at constant speed with a force of 10 N at $30 ^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Find the work done against friction.
back:
At constant speed the friction equals the horizontal component of the pull, so the work done against friction is the work done by that component:

$W = 10 \times 5 \times \mathrm{cos} 30 ^{\circ} = 43 . 3 \text{J}$

The mass of the box plays no part, because the vertical direction is never used.

front: In this course, what is meant by **mechanical energy**?
back:
**Mechanical energy** is the kind of energy dealt with in mechanics, as distinct from heat, light, chemical or nuclear energy.

It exists in two forms: **kinetic energy (KE)** and **gravitational potential energy (GPE)**.

front:
A particle of mass $m$ kg moves with speed $v \text{m s}^{-1}$. Fill in the blanks to complete its kinetic energy:

`\text{KE} = \_\_\_\_\_\_ m v^{\_\_\_\_\_\_}`
back:
The completed formula is:

$\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$

A particle has kinetic energy only while it is moving, and this is one of the formulae you are expected to know rather than look up.

front: Kinetic energy is a scalar. What does that tell you about its sign, and what unit is it measured in?
back:
It can **never be negative**, which the formula guarantees, since $v^{2}$ is never negative whichever way the particle is travelling.

It is measured in **joules (J)**, with $1 \text{kJ} = 1000 \text{J}$.

front: How do you find the change in kinetic energy, and what is the common mistake?
back:
Subtract the initial kinetic energy from the final one:

`\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} - \frac{1}{2}mu^{2} = \frac{1}{2}m\left( v^{2} - u^{2} \right)`

The mistake is to use the difference of the **speeds** where the difference of their **squares** is wanted: $v^{2} - u^{2}$ is not `\left( v - u \right)^{2}`.

front: A particle moves in two dimensions with velocity vector $v$. What are the two ways to find its kinetic energy?
back:
Find the **speed** as the magnitude of $v$, then put that single number into the formula.

Or apply the formula to each **component** separately and add the two results together.

front: A jogger's speed rises from $2 \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $3 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and her kinetic energy increases by 150 J. Find her mass.
back:
Use the difference of the squares of the speeds:

`\frac{1}{2}m\left( 3^{2} - 2^{2} \right) = 150`

That gives $\frac{5}{2} m = 150$, so the jogger's mass is $60 \text{kg}$.

front: What is gravitational potential energy, and what is the formula for it?
back:
**Gravitational potential energy** is the energy an object has because of its **height** above a chosen fixed level, with gravity acting on it.

It is the weight multiplied by that height, $\text{GPE} = m g h$, measured in **joules** when $m$ is in kilograms and $h$ in metres.

front: An object is dragged up a slope. Which height goes into $m g h$, and what if you are given the slant distance?
back:
The **vertical** height gained, never the distance travelled along the slope.

If the question gives you the slant distance, use trigonometry on the angle of the slope to find the vertical rise first.

front:
**True or False?**

An object resting on the chosen base level has zero gravitational potential energy.
back:
**True.**

Height is measured from whatever fixed level has been chosen as the base, so $h = 0$ there and $m g h = 0$.

That also means gravitational potential energy is not an absolute quantity: move the base level and every value changes, which is why problems turn on **changes** in it.

front:
Fill in the blanks to complete the work-energy principle, written as an energy balance:

total final energy $=$ total `\_\_\_\_\_\_` energy $\pm$ work done by `\_\_\_\_\_\_` forces.
back:
The completed principle is:

total final energy $=$ total **initial** energy $\pm$ work done by **non-gravitational** forces.

It is an energy balance, rather like a bank account: the final amount is the initial amount plus whatever was put in or taken out.

front: In the work-energy principle, what does "total energy" mean?
back:
The **sum of the gravitational potential energy and the kinetic energy**, worked out at each of the two instants.

So each side of the balance is of the form $m g h + \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$, one with the initial values and one with the final ones.

front: Why is the weight $m g$ left out of the "work done by non-gravitational forces" term?
back:
Because the work done against gravity has **already been counted**, inside the gravitational potential energy part of the total energy.

Putting the weight into the work-done term as well would count the same energy **twice**.

The forces that do belong there are friction, tensions, driving forces and air resistance.

front: In the work-energy principle, when do you add the work done and when do you subtract it?
back:
**Add** it for forces that help the object move forwards, such as a driving force or a tension pulling it along.

**Subtract** it for forces that hinder the motion, such as friction, air resistance or a tension pulling backwards.

Where several such forces act, add or subtract each one according to which it does.

front:
**True or False?**

The "change in KE $=$ minus change in GPE $\pm$ work done" form works in every situation without adaptation.
back:
**False.**

That gain-and-loss form has to be adapted to each situation, and it is where most **sign errors** come from, because a "gain" is sometimes negative.

The energy-balance form, final $=$ initial $\pm$ work done, is written the same way every time and works in every situation.

front: Define **conservation of energy**.
back:
**Conservation of energy** is the special case of the work-energy principle in which **no work is done by non-gravitational forces**.

The balance then reduces to total final energy $=$ total initial energy, with no extra term at all.

front: Give the two ways a situation can have no work done by non-gravitational forces.
back:
There may be **none acting**, as for a particle falling freely under gravity from a fixed height.

Or every one of them may act **perpendicular to the direction of motion**, as the normal reaction does on an object moving along a horizontal surface.

front: A particle is fired horizontally at $8 \text{m s}^{-1}$ off a 30 m cliff and moves freely under gravity. Use energy to find its speed on impact.
back:
Nothing but gravity acts, so the total energy is unchanged and the gravitational potential energy lost becomes kinetic energy gained:

$\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m \times 8^{2} + m g \times 30$

The mass cancels throughout, leaving $v^{2} = 64 + 588 = 652$, so the speed of impact is $25 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ to 3 significant figures.

front: Define **power**.
back:
**Power** is the **rate of doing work**, that is the work done per second, usually by the driving force of an engine.

It is a scalar quantity and can only be positive.

front:
A driving force of $F$ N acts on an object moving at $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, doing $\text{WD}$ joules of work in $t$ seconds. Fill in the blanks to complete the two formulae for power:

`P = \frac{\_\_\_\_\_\_}{t} = \_\_\_\_\_\_`
back:
The completed formulae are:

$P = \frac{\text{WD}}{t} = F v$

The second form is the more useful in vehicle questions, and it requires the velocity to be in the **same direction** as the force.

front:
**True or False?**

The force in $P = F v$ is the resultant force on the vehicle.
back:
**False.**

It is the **driving force** of the engine alone, since power is what the engine develops as it converts fuel into that force.

The resistance forces belong in the equation of motion, but they must be kept out of this formula.

front: How is $P = F v$ obtained from $P = \frac{\text{WD}}{t}$?
back:
The work done by a constant force $F$ over a distance $s$ is $F s$, so the power is $\frac{Fs}{t}$.

Since $\frac{s}{t}$ is the speed $v$, that is simply $F v$.

front: What are the units of power?
back:
**Watts (W)**, where 1 watt is 1 joule per second.

Larger powers are given in **kilowatts**, with $1 \text{kW} = 1000 \text{W}$, so check which the question wants before giving an answer.

front: Why does a vehicle working at maximum power eventually reach a maximum speed?
back:
With $P$ fixed at its maximum, $P = F v$ means the **driving force falls as the speed rises**.

Eventually the driving force has fallen to equal the resistance, so the resultant force is zero.

By Newton's second law the acceleration is then zero, and the speed stops increasing.

front: A car of mass 1300 kg meets a constant resistance of 900 N and has a maximum speed of $40 \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find its maximum power, and say why the mass is not needed.
back:
At maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force equals the resistance, 900 N:

$P = F v = 900 \times 40 = 36000 \text{W} = 36 \text{kW}$

The mass is not needed because zero acceleration makes $m a$ zero, so the mass never enters the equation of motion.
